title.ja: ラスボスは、小さな一枚

synopsis: Tom brings an oversized katakana "final boss" game to the class, all spectacle and dramatic battle framing. Running it means reading the cards at speed, counting the pieces, and following his live commands. But the giant boss card refuses to win, and Felix is the only one still watching a tiny paper cat clipped to the smallest, least dramatic card. When the marked card is finally read, it settles the game — and Tom hands the spectacle over to another person's quiet find.

scenes.goal: Run Tom's oversized katakana game by reading the cards, counting the pieces, and following his commands.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will the game be won by the biggest, most dramatic card, or by reading the cards at all?
scenes.learnerNeed: A live play loop that forces katakana to be read by shape, pieces to be counted, and spoken commands to be followed — with no English gloss to lean on.

nodes.description: Tom clears the front desk and lays out an oversized card game. Five big katakana cards stand in a row, three round tokens beside them. One card towers over the rest, hand-labelled ボス. On the battered game box, a small photo sticker of a dog is captioned チェスナットさん. Clipped to the smallest, plainest card at the edge is a folded paper cat, easy to miss.

nodes.intent: Unveil the game as a dramatic final-boss battle and issue the first command to start play by drawing one card.
nodes.attentionTarget: the towering ボス card at the centre of the row

nodes.resume: The five katakana cards, three tokens, and two players are laid out. Tom's commands to draw and look are on the table, and the learner steps in to read and run the game.

nodes.resumeContext: Five katakana cards are face up (ボス and four others, including a small plain one reading ネコ). The learner runs the play loop by reading each card by shape rather than reaching for an English gloss, counting the pieces with the right counters (〜まい for cards, 〜つ/〜こ for tokens, 〜り/〜にん for players), and following Tom's spoken commands (ひいてください / みてください) to select the card he names.

nodes.description: Only the card that was misread turns back face up on its own; the cards already read correctly stay where the learner placed them. No English gloss appears — just the katakana, a little larger, waiting to be read again.

nodes.resume: The cards have been read and counted, and Tom's named card was selected by reading it. The boss card is finally drawn — and the game does not end.

nodes.intent: Admit that drawing the giant boss card, the whole centrepiece of his spectacle, does not win the game.
nodes.attentionTarget: the huge ボス card, now drawn but resolving nothing

nodes.description: The ボス card stands drawn and enormous at the centre, and the game sits stalled around it. At the edge of the table, unmoved, the folded paper cat still marks the smallest, plainest card.

scenes.goal: Let the game be settled by reading the smallest, paper-cat-marked card instead of by the biggest gesture.
scenes.dramaticQuestion: Will spectacle make room for another person's quiet find, or keep insisting on the boss?
scenes.learnerNeed: A stance on who reads the one small card that actually decides the game, once reading it — not drawing the boss — is what matters.

nodes.description: The class has crowded in around the giant ボス card, arguing about how to beat it. At the edge of the table, the small card with the folded paper cat sits untouched, its plain katakana facing up and unread.

nodes.intent: Turn the class from the giant card back to the small one the paper cat marks, and ask for it to be read by its katakana.
nodes.attentionTarget: the folded paper cat and the small card it marks, reading ネコ

n2.english: You read it. "Neko." That's the win. The plainest, smallest card of the lot. …Not the flashy push — the one card you quietly read is what wins. That's the game it was, all along.

n1.japanese: ちゃんと読めましたね。「ネコ」。はい、これで勝ちです。よりによって一番地味で、一番小さいカード。…結局、一番派手なひと押しじゃなくて、静かに一枚読めたほうが勝つ。そういう作りだったんですよ、これ。

n1.english: You read it properly. "Neko." Right, that's the win. Of all things, the plainest and smallest card. …In the end, it's not the flashiest push that wins — it's quietly reading one card. That's how this thing was built, it turns out.

nodes.intent: Take quiet delight that the small marker was the whole game, and wave off his own noticing as luck rather than skill.
nodes.attentionTarget: the paper cat resting on the winning small card

foundation.reading: よかった。ねこが、ただしかったですね。ぼく、うんがよかっただけです。
foundation.english: Good. The cat was right. I just got lucky.

nodes.description: The giant ボス card is set aside, face down. In the middle of the table sits the small card reading ネコ, face up, the folded paper cat resting on top of it. On the game box, the little dog sticker captioned チェスナットさん watches over the whole thing.

callbacks.meaningNow: A tiny paper cat marks the least dramatic clue in Tom's oversized game — the smallest card, not the biggest gesture, is what matters. Reading the marked card, rather than drawing the boss, is what settles the game.
callbacks.optionalFallback: The game is simply decided by a small marked card that has to be read, rather than by the biggest card being drawn; the paper marker can be a neutral clip if the cat motif is withdrawn.

outcomes.description: Tom's oversized katakana final-boss game is won not by drawing the giant boss card but by reading the smallest, paper-cat-marked card (ネコ); the boss card is set aside and the marked small card stays face up as the decider.

Tom arrives as the class's methodical-showman: he stages an oversized final-boss spectacle and counts every piece for fun, then, in the same evening, lets that spectacle make room for Felix's quiet find — softening from performing the big gesture toward handing the win to the smallest true thing.

Read-or-select-a-katakana-item-without-translation-first evidence returns through the registered transfer activity, alongside counters and light commands run as a live play loop; the story emits no lesson-completion command.

replay.withdrawnContentFallback: Run the same read-and-run play loop and small-marked-card resolution with neutral nameplates and a generic pair who read katakana, count the pieces, and settle the game on the smallest marked card after the boss card fails to win.
